approach_variants.name: Boston Basin climbers' trail and Quien Sabe Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to camp, 3-4 more to the col
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.
hazards: Missing the sharp right turn off the mine roadbed onto the climbers' trail
Bergschrund at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, open both sides late season
Rockfall from the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower during the rising traverse
Exposed knife-edge ridge above the col
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The rock climbing begins at the Boston-Sahale col, and everything below it is glacier work.

The navigational problem on the way up is the bergschrund, at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides late season. Late in the year the standard solution is to traverse climber's right to end-run the schrund, then cut back up and left above it to the col — a party that pushes straight up the fall line into the schrund is not off route so much as too early in the season for that line.

You know you are at the col because the glacier ends against a defined saddle in the rock ridge and the ground on the far side drops away toward Boston Peak. This is where parties unrope and coil.

From the col the route is the ridge: it steepens, then widens, then narrows to an exposed class 3-4 knife edge. At the high point of that ridge the false summit comes into view ahead of you — that view is the confirmation that you have done the ridge section correctly and are approaching the summit block. The block is then finished as on the Sahale Glacier route, on ledges around the east side to a short class 4 exit at a fixed rappel station.

In poor visibility the col itself is the reliable target: it is the only low saddle at the top of the glacier, and the ridge beyond it cannot be confused with glacier travel.
